questions.raw_text: Discuss the properties of diamond and graphite and relate them to their internal structures.

stem.text: Discuss the properties of diamond and graphite and relate them to their internal structures.

topic_names: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon with different physical properties due to different bonding. In diamond, each carbon is bonded to four others in a rigid, three-dimensional structure, making it the hardest known substance. In graphite, each carbon bonds with three others in the same plane, forming layers of hexagonal arrays. This structural difference allows graphite to be smooth and slippery, unlike diamond. Furthermore, graphite is a good conductor of electricity due to its specific bonding arrangement, whereas diamond is not.

questions.raw_text: Compare the nature of chemical bonding in ionic compounds versus carbon (covalent) compounds, particularly regarding their physical properties.

stem.text: Compare the nature of chemical bonding in ionic compounds versus carbon (covalent) compounds, particularly regarding their physical properties.

topic_names: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points and conduct electricity in their molten or solution states because they consist of charged ions. In contrast, carbon compounds rely on the sharing of valence electrons to form covalent bonds. These compounds exhibit low melting and boiling points because the intermolecular forces between the molecules are weak. Additionally, because the electrons are shared to form neutral, non-charged molecules, carbon compounds are typically poor conductors of electricity compared to ionic compounds.

questions.raw_text: Discuss the necessity of electron sharing in carbon and briefly describe how it forms bonds with other elements like hydrogen.

stem.text: Discuss the necessity of electron sharing in carbon and briefly describe how it forms bonds with other elements like hydrogen.

topic_names: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: Carbon has four electrons in its outer shell; to attain a noble gas configuration, it must lose or gain four electrons. Forming a C4- anion is impractical as the six-proton nucleus struggles to hold ten electrons, and forming a C4+ cation requires excessive energy to remove four electrons. Carbon resolves this by sharing its valence electrons with other atoms. For example, in methane (CH4), carbon shares its four valence electrons with four hydrogen atoms, resulting in each atom achieving a stable configuration through the formation of covalent bonds.

questions.raw_text: Explain, using examples, why bonds between atoms can range from single to triple.

stem.text: Explain, using examples, why bonds between atoms can range from single to triple.

topic_names: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: The type of covalent bond depends on how many electron pairs are shared between atoms. A single bond is formed when one pair of electrons is shared, as seen in hydrogen (H2), where each atom contributes one electron. A double bond is formed when two pairs of electrons are shared (four total), as in oxygen (O2), where each oxygen atom shares two of its six valence electrons to complete its octet. A triple bond is formed when three pairs of electrons are shared (six total), as in nitrogen (N2), where each nitrogen atom contributes three electrons to attain an octet.

questions.raw_text: Describe the occurrence of carbon in nature and explain its universal significance in organic structures.

stem.text: Describe the occurrence of carbon in nature and explain its universal significance in organic structures.

topic_names: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: Carbon exists in nature in relatively small amounts: the Earth's crust contains 0.02% in minerals like carbonates and petroleum, and the atmosphere holds 0.03% carbon dioxide. Despite this, its significance is immense as it serves as the foundation for the versatile carbon-based chemistry found in all living structures. Furthermore, carbon is vital to modern society as it comprises the base of food, medicines, books, and fuels. The ability of carbon to form stable covalent bonds with other elements and other carbon atoms allows for the immense diversity of compounds essential for life.
